items.prompt: Evaluate this claim about the chapter: “The marriage rescues the family's reputation but not Lydia's happiness.” Is it fully persuasive? Argue with evidence, including a passage that complicates it.
items.expected: The claim is persuasive only in part. In support, “neither rational happiness nor worldly prosperity, could be justly expected for her sister” (Chapter XLIX, paragraph 56) bears it out: Mrs. Bennet rejoices "Mrs. Wickham! How well it sounds," while Elizabeth sees that "neither rational happiness nor worldly prosperity" can be expected for Lydia. But “His consenting to marry her is a proof, I will believe, that he is come to a right way of thinking” (Chapter XLIX, paragraph 42) complicates it, because this detail (jane's charitable hope) gives the reader a second explanation to weigh against the claim's reading. So the claim holds only once it is qualified: it explains much of the chapter, but it has to account for that passage too, which it does not do on its own.
